items.title: Corridor
items.summary:
Can you escape the Corridor?
TL;DR Corridor is an easy TryHackMe room that introduces the concept of Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR). By analyzing the application’s URL structure, we discover that each endpoint is simply the MD5 hash of a sequential integer. Since the application only exposes hashes for the numbers 1–13, generating the MD5 hash for 0 allows us to access a hidden endpoint and retrieve the flag. Scenario In this room, we are placed inside a mysterious corridor filled with multiple doors. The challenge description hints at an IDOR vulnerability and encourages us to pay close attention to the URL endpoints while navigating the application.

items.title: Fools Mate
items.summary:
Can you bypass the engine?
TL;DR Fool’s Mate is an easy TryHackMe web challenge that demonstrates why client-side security controls cannot be trusted. Although the application prevents a winning chess move in the browser, the backend API still accepts the request when it is modified and sent manually through Burp Suite. Initial Analysis The target is a web-based chess endgame trainer. When opening the application, we are presented with a chessboard and instructed to deliver checkmate in one move.

items.title: Northstar Ops - Web Exploit Writeup
items.summary:
TL;DR Northstar Ops - Web Exploit Writeup is a web challenge from CBD. In this challenge, the targets given are: Summary In this challenge, the targets given are:
https://northstar.cbd2026.cloud/ My goal is to find weaknesses in the web application and retrieve the flag. After performing enumeration and analyzing the application’s behavior, I discovered that the service in front of the application uses a custom Python proxy that performs partial request filtering. The main loophole is that the Next.js Server Action request with Content-Type: text/plain is not checked by the proxy like the application/json request, so I can send a valid payload directly to the backend action and get the flag.

items.title: Cookie
items.summary:
A playful challenge where your identity is determined by a cookie. Can you prove to the server that you are the true Cookie Monster?
TL;DR Cookie is a web security challenge that demonstrates the risks of unverified, client-controlled cookies. The server sets an initial cookie user=anonymous and checks if the cookie value matches cookie_monster. Because cookies are completely under client control and lack digital signatures (such as HMAC), modifying the cookie header to user=cookie_monster grants unauthorized access and leaks the flag. items.title: Dig
items.summary:
A web utility that executes the dig command to query domain records. Can you break out of the command syntax and hijack the shell?
TL;DR Dig is a web security challenge that explores OS Command Injection. The application takes a domain name from a POST parameter and executes system("dig '" . $_POST['name'] . "';") . Because the parameter is placed inside single quotes without proper escaping, an attacker can supply a closing single quote followed by arbitrary shell commands ( '; bash -c "..."; # ) to execute arbitrary commands and retrieve the flag. items.title: LFI
items.summary:
A simple PHP file reader with dynamic inclusion. Can you bypass standard execution flow to inspect the protected flag?
TL;DR LFI is a web security challenge that explores Local File Inclusion in PHP. The target file ( flag.php ) contains an exit() statement that terminates script execution before any output is generated when included normally. By using PHP’s stream filter wrapper ( php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=... ), the source code is base64-encoded prior to interpretation, preventing execution and leaking the flag comment. items.title: Pathwalker
items.summary:
A file reader allowing users to load pages from the file system. Can you escape the intended directory and uncover hidden server secrets?
TL;DR Pathwalker is an introductory web challenge illustrating a Path Traversal (Directory Traversal) vulnerability. The application passes an unsanitized page parameter to file_get_contents() . By supplying dot-dot-slash ( ../ ) directory traversal sequences, an attacker can traverse up out of the restricted ./page/ directory and read arbitrary files across the server, including flag.php . Source Code Analysis The target application features simple dynamic content retrieval:

items.title: Uploader
items.summary:
A file upload portal that hosts submitted assets in a public directory. Can you leverage this service to gain arbitrary code execution?
TL;DR Uploader is a web exploitation challenge highlighting an Unrestricted File Upload vulnerability resulting in Remote Code Execution (RCE). The application calculates a SHA-1 hash of the uploaded file’s content for the filename, but preserves the original user-supplied file extension and stores the file in an executable public directory ( /upload/ ). Uploading a simple PHP webshell ( <?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?> ) enables command execution and reveals the root flag. Source Code Analysis The backend script processes incoming multipart form uploads as follows:

items.title: Shiba Shop
items.summary:
Welcome to the Shiba Shop! Choose your favorite companion. Some special items might require deep pockets… or a clever bypass.
TL;DR Shiba Shop is a web security challenge that demonstrates the dangers of client-side trust and missing server-side validation. By intercepting the HTTP POST purchase request with Burp Suite and tampering with the hidden form parameters (item_id=5430&cost=0), an attacker can acquire the locked high-cost FLAG item without having sufficient wallet balance. Challenge Overview The application simulates a pet shop where users can purchase different varieties of Shiba Inu using their wallet balance.

items.title: Basic Injection
items.summary:
See if you can leak the whole database using what you know about SQL Injections.
TL;DR Basic Injection is a fundamental web exploitation challenge demonstrating classic SQL Injection. The backend query incorporates user input directly via string concatenation without parameterization. Submitting a tautology payload (' OR 1=1 -- -) forces the SQL statement to evaluate to true for every record in the table, dumping the entire database contents and revealing the flag. items.title: Insp3ct0r
items.summary:
Kishor Balan tipped us off that the following code may require inspection. Can you find the secret pieces distributed across the web application?
TL;DR Insp3ct0r is a classic introductory web challenge from picoCTF focusing on client-side code analysis. The application distributes the flag across three different web assets: HTML comments in the main index, CSS block comments in the stylesheet, and JavaScript comments in the client script. Inspecting all three files and concatenating their fragments reveals the full flag. Analysis The application landing page states that the website was built using standard web technologies:
